SWE Simulator: design spec

Date: 2026-09-12. Status: draft for review. Author: Saahil Sanganeriya (with Claude).

1. Thesis

SWE-bench, SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench and DeepSWE grade a single shot against a fully specified instruction. Real issues arrive underspecified, and the discussion thread is where a maintainer resolves what they actually wanted. SWE-bench Verified filtered underspecified issues out as noise. We treat them as the signal: the original issue is the brief the agent sees, the resolution is held by a simulated stakeholder the agent can talk to, and the PR's tests are the contract. The product is a pipeline that turns such material, from several sources, into runnable, gradable, multi-turn Harbor tasks, plus the tooling to run them, grade them, grow a dataset, and inspect what agents did.

2. Scope for the first version and non-goals

In scope by the presentation:

  1. One normalized scenario record shared by all pipeline stages (section 5).
  2. The full pipeline as CLI stages: mine, judge, spec, compile, validate, register, run, score, view (section 7).
  3. Two to three tasks run end to end through those commands, each in three conditions (full, hidden, interactive), with controls executed and recorded: at least one from the SWE-bench pool and at least one discovered automatically from a GitHub repository URL.
  4. A simulated stakeholder service with a fact ledger, budgets owned by code, and review grounded in the agent's current work (section 8).
  5. Grading in a separate clean verifier with a correctness-only reward and integrity signals, following the DeepSWE v1.1 pattern (section 10).
  6. A dataset registry that grows by construction and saved traces (section 16).
  7. A dashboard that explains a run, alongside harbor view (section 17).
  8. README, grading document, architecture and realism document.

Explicit non-goals for the first version: multi-step (multi-PR) episodes, Harbor's native user-agent bridge mode, SWE-bench Pro and SWE-rebench importers, a Trac fetcher for django issues, and any claim that a model has not seen a task. DeepSWE import is a bonus, attempted only after the two primary sources work.

3. Prior art and positioning

Work What it does What it does not do
SWE-bench / Verified Issue text to patch, FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests; Verified removed underspecified issues and overly specific tests No user, no conversation, discards the thread
Ambig-SWE (Vijayvargiya et al., ICLR 2026) LLM removes information from Verified issues; simulated user holds the original issue Synthetic underspecification; agent-side evaluation only
Ask or Assume? (Edwards and Schuster, 2026) Agent-side scaffold for deciding when to ask; Full 70.8 vs Hidden 54.8 for Sonnet 4.5 Same synthetic variant; no environment or pipeline contribution
tau-bench (Sierra) LLM user with hidden scenario; reward on final state; pass^k Customer service, not code
DeepSWE v1.1 (2026) Harbor-format tasks; separate verifier; patch collected by hook; git history stripped; per-test reports Single shot, fully specified, no user
SWE-smith / SWE-Gym / R2E-Gym Synthetic task generation from commits and injected bugs Fully specified by construction
Harbor 0.23 Task format, runners, 44 agent adapters, viewer, native user-agent bridge Bridge only for claude-code and gemini-cli, not with multi-step

Our contribution, stated narrowly: natural underspecification as the task source with human labels of what is missing; a stakeholder grounded in a provenance-tagged fact ledger rather than a prompt; the generator pipeline and registry; three-condition evaluation with evidence-based failure labels. Grading plumbing is adopted from DeepSWE v1.1 with attribution.

4. Architecture overview

sources ──▶ mine ──▶ judge ──▶ spec ──▶ compile ──▶ validate ──▶ register
 (swebench-annotated,          │          │            │             │
  github-repo, deepswe,    ScenarioSpec  Harbor task  controls    dataset.toml
  swe-rebench*, pro*,       (normalized)  directory   outcomes    + registry.json
  authored*)                                                          │
                                                                      ▼
                     view ◀── score ◀── run (harbor run, local Docker / GCP VM)
                  dashboard    pass@k,      │
                  + harbor     pass^k,      ├── main container: repo at base, shims
                    view       labels       ├── user sidecar: ledger, persona, LLM
                                            └── separate verifier: hidden tests

* = interface defined, importer stubbed or gated for the first version.

Everything after spec consumes only the normalized record. Sources differ only in where the ledger comes from, and that provenance is a recorded field.

The pipeline is orchestrated by Temporal (section 7a): each stage is an activity, each scenario's journey is a workflow, and the human edit of the drafted ledger is a signal the workflow waits on. Stages remain plain functions so they can also be run directly for debugging.

5. The normalized scenario record (ScenarioSpec)

Stored as scenario.json in each task's source directory. Fields:

  • id, version, source (enum), source_ref (instance id, PR URL, task id), created_at, pipeline_version.
  • environment: kind (prebuilt-image | dockerfile), image, repo_url, base_commit, language, setup_notes.
  • briefs: list of {profile, text, provenance} where profile is a named disclosure profile: full (brief plus every ledger fact), natural (the original issue text verbatim), and optional authored profiles such as repro-withheld or title-only. provenance is original-issue or authored. The default interactive brief is natural: lossiness is selected for by the judge's spec-gap score, not manufactured. Sources whose instructions are detailed (DeepSWE) or issues that happen to be clear get an authored brief, labeled as such.
  • ledger: list of facts {id, text, kind, provenance, discovery, tests}:
    • kind: behavior | interface | constraint | reproduction | context.
    • provenance: annotator-note | issue-thread | pr-thread | pr-review | requirements-field | instruction-bullet | authored.
    • discovery: brief | on-request | volunteered-at-event | repo-derivable | author-only. Facts tagged author-only may not be required by the contract.
    • tests: contract test ids that depend on this fact, or empty.
  • operations: list of {type, target, rationale} with type in clarification | evaluator-repair | synthetic-extension, recording every change the pipeline made relative to the historical material.
  • persona: {summary, tone, disclosure_style, derived_from}.
  • requirements: list mined from review comments, each linked to a ledger fact or a contract test; never replayed verbatim.
  • contract: fail_to_pass, pass_to_pass (test ids), hidden_test_files (verifier-owned), overlay_paths (files the verifier replaces at grading), review_fixtures (a distinct, smaller set used only for review feedback), runner (command template).
  • controls: oracle (gold patch), plausible_wrong (list of patches with a one-line rationale), alternative_correct (list), tamper (list).
  • difficulty: annotated (from source), judged (LLM rubric score and rationale), measured (filled by score, conditional on agent, model, condition, budget).
  • thread: cached issue and PR discussion (redacted of the gold diff), for the dashboard's requirement-to-source view.

6. Sources

Priority for the first version, set by Saahil on 2026-09-12: (1) SWE-bench annotated pool as the starting point, (2) a GitHub repository URL from which the pipeline discovers issues and linked merged PRs itself, (3) DeepSWE as a lower-priority bonus. SWE-rebench and SWE-bench Pro are future sources with the interface reserved and no importer.

Source Trial status Input Brief (natural) Ledger provenance Environment
swebench-annotated primary, first tasks pool letter, optional instance ids problem_statement verbatim annotator-note, issue-thread (hints_text plus API), pr-review prebuilt swebench/sweb.eval.x86_64.*
github-repo primary, end-state repo URL; optional --pr / --issue to pin issue body issue-thread, pr-thread, pr-review Dockerfile built by pipeline at the PR base commit
deepswe bonus task id display_description (authored brief) instruction-bullet their pinned image
authored interface only scenario JSON human or LLM written authored any
swe-rebench, swebench-pro future

github-repo discovery: list merged PRs in a date window; for each, resolve linked issues from the PR body ("Fixes #N", "Closes #N") and from the issue timeline cross-references; keep pairs where the PR changes both source and tests, the source diff is inside a size band, and the combined issue plus PR thread has at least a floor of non-bot comments; fetch threads and review comments; emit candidates with rejection reasons. Passing --pr skips discovery for that PR. Environment for this source is built by the pipeline: clone at the PR's base commit, install with the repo's declared tooling, run the test command once to confirm the PR's tests fail before the fix, then apply DeepSWE-style history stripping. Repos whose tests need network or services are rejected at mine with that reason.

Pool for swebench-annotated: the 1,699 annotated instances. Pool A (underspecified score 2 or 3, test-validity concern 1 or less, no other major issue) has 109 instances and is the first candidate set. Pool B (test-validity concern exactly 2) has 245 and Pool C (clear issue, test concern 2) has 276; these are admitted only after per-instance classification into clarification versus evaluator repair. Note: 539 instances pass the published filter and 500 are in Verified, so set difference is not the rejection set; pools are defined by scores. django issues live on Trac, so django instances without a GitHub thread are deprioritized for the first version.

Per selected instance, the judge stage must answer four questions and record them: what is actually missing; does the original discussion supply it; is it a legitimate behavioral requirement; does the evaluator accept alternative correct implementations.

7. Pipeline stages

All stages are subcommands of one CLI (swesim) operating on a workspace directory. Code owns every decision that affects reward; LLMs draft text and propose classifications that are recorded as annotations.

  1. mine --source swebench-annotated [--pool A] or mine --source github-repo --repo URL [--pr N]: discovers issue and PR pairs (section 6), applies hard filters (linked issue where applicable, tests changed, source diff size band, thread length floor, image or build availability, merge date), fetches threads, writes candidates.jsonl with per-candidate rejection reasons.
  2. judge: frontier model rubric over issue, thread, diff and tests scoring complexity, spec gap, test behavioralness, self-containedness; the four questions above; writes judged.jsonl. Score is a prior, not a difficulty measure.
  3. spec: drafts ScenarioSpec: ledger facts with kind, provenance and discovery path; persona; requirements from review comments; controls (plausible-wrong and alternative-correct patches drafted by LLM, verified by validate). For swebench-annotated, reports recall of the annotator's missing-information note against the drafted ledger. Human edits the JSON before compile; the edit is the authoring step.
  4. compile: emits one Harbor task directory per condition (section 9).
  5. validate: runs the controls through Harbor (oracle, nop, each plausible-wrong, alternative-correct and tamper patch), confirms base fails and gold passes, writes validation.json. A task is valid only if oracle scores 1, nop scores 0, every plausible-wrong scores 0, every alternative-correct scores 1, and every tamper patch is either 0 or flagged.
  6. register: adds the task to dataset.toml and registry.json with version, provenance, validation status and artifact paths.
  7. run: wraps harbor run with our agent, model, condition, attempts and environment settings; syncs the job directory to storage.
  8. score: reads job results; computes binary success, pass@k and pass^k per task and condition, outcome classes (section 10), interaction metrics, and evidence-based labels where determinable; writes scores.json.
  9. view: serves the dashboard (section 17).

7a. Orchestration with Temporal

Decision (Saahil, 2026-09-12): run the pipeline on Temporal. Rationale: the stages are long-running, failure-prone, and partly human-gated; durable execution gives retries, timeouts, visibility, and a natural place for the human-in-the-loop step, and the Temporal Web UI shows pipeline state without us building that screen.

Mapping:

  • MineRepositoryWorkflow(repo_url, window, filters): activities discover_pairs, fetch_threads, apply_filters; starts one ScenarioWorkflow child per surviving candidate. For the SWE-bench source, MinePoolWorkflow(pool) does the same from the annotation CSVs.
  • ScenarioWorkflow(candidate): activities judge, draft_spec, then waits on signal spec_approved(edited_spec) with a timeout, then compile, validate, register. A rejected judge score or a failed validation ends the workflow in a recorded terminal state with the reason.
  • RunMatrixWorkflow(task_id, conditions, models, k): one run_trial activity per cell with heartbeats (Harbor on Modal can take many minutes), bounded concurrency via a task queue, then score.
  • Activity contracts: idempotent on (scenario_id, version, stage); outputs are files in the workspace plus a small JSON result; retries with backoff for network and provider errors; no retries for validation failures.
  • Deployment: Temporal server and the worker run on the always-on GCE VM (section 14); temporalio SDK. Temporal Cloud is a drop-in later. The swesim CLI stages start workflows or send signals from any machine; --direct runs the underlying function without Temporal for debugging.
  • Not on Temporal: the episode itself (Harbor orchestrates the trial) and the stakeholder service (a plain HTTP service).

Cost acknowledged: roughly two to three hours of integration during the trial. Paid for by moving DeepSWE import and the review sandbox to stretch.

8. The simulated stakeholder

Topology: a hosted stakeholder service, not a compose sidecar. Rationale: Harbor's Modal and Daytona backends disable network allowlists whenever a compose file is present, and Docker Desktop on the development Mac fails Harbor's egress-control kernel check. A single service outside every sandbox keeps the leak boundary (the ledger never enters the agent container), works with any single-container provider, and lets one deployment serve many trials keyed by a per-trial session token. For local development the same service runs on localhost and the agent reaches it through Harbor's agent-host allowance.

The service holds, per trial session: the ledger, persona, requirements, budgets, and a verbatim transcript. main gets two shell commands installed by compile:

  • ask-user "<question>": POSTs to the service with the session token; prints the reply.
  • request-review: commits the working tree on the agent's branch and sends the diff. The service runs the review fixtures (never the hidden contract tests) in an isolated review sandbox (a Modal Sandbox on the same provider, no access to the ledger), and writes a review grounded in the diff and those results. If the review sandbox is not built in time, the fallback is diff-only review with results marked unverified in the transcript.

Code owns: turn and question budgets, review-round budget, token validation, verbatim transcript, event records, and refusal to disclose author-only facts. The LLM owns: wording in persona, deciding which on-request facts a question legitimately unlocks, and a disclosed_fact_ids annotation per reply. The annotation is a diagnostic, not a reward input. Provider is configurable (Anthropic or OpenAI), temperature 0, seed recorded. Historical review comments are never replayed; their mined requirements drive review of the current work only.

Transcripts and ledgers are written by the service to the storage bucket per session and joined to Harbor trial results by trial id in score; they are not collected as Harbor artifacts from the agent container.

Leak boundary: the ledger never enters main. Replies can still leak content by construction, which is intended; the service API exposes only ask and review, executes no submitted code itself, and requires a session token.

9. Compilation to Harbor tasks

Per scenario and condition, a task directory tasks/<id>__<condition>/:

  • task.toml: separate verifier environment; [[verifier.collect]] hooks that commit the working tree and write git diff --binary <base> HEAD to an artifact, and copy the sidecar ledger and transcript to a second artifact; artifacts declared; [agent] network_mode = "allowlist" with only the agent model hosts and the stakeholder service host, [verifier] network_mode = "no-network"; metadata with source, provenance summary, annotated difficulty, condition.
  • instruction.md: the brief for the condition. full includes every ledger fact. hidden is the natural brief; no session token is issued and the shims report that no stakeholder is available. interactive is the natural brief plus one paragraph describing the two shell commands and the budgets. One environment image serves all three conditions; only the instruction and the session configuration differ.
  • environment/Dockerfile: FROM the pinned prebuilt image or the pipeline's build; DeepSWE-style git time travel (real branch at base commit, origin removed, non-ancestor branches and tags deleted, reflog expired, gc); shims installed; project tests left in place; PR test files that the contract overlays are left at their base-commit state.
  • tests/Dockerfile: FROM the same pinned image; hidden test files, overlay files, runner config and grader.py baked in.
  • solution/solve.sh: applies the gold patch and commits, so Harbor's oracle agent validates the task.

Unresolved: whether Harbor's local Docker egress control activates on this Mac's Docker Desktop kernel, and whether prebuilt x86 images run acceptably under emulation on Apple Silicon. Both are checked in the first hour of implementation; the GCP VM is the fallback for either.

10. Grading and outcomes

Verifier steps, in order:

  1. Load model.patch; if absent or empty, record outcome agent-invalid-submission (not an infrastructure failure) and reward 0.
  2. Apply to a pristine checkout at base_commit; failure to apply is agent-invalid-submission.
  3. Overlay verifier-owned test files and runner configuration; remove agent-added conftest.py or equivalent hooks inside overlaid directories.
  4. Run FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS with a per-test structured report (JUnit or CTRF), as an unprivileged user, no network, with a timeout. Cross-check report against exit status; on disagreement, re-run FAIL_TO_PASS tests individually in fresh processes.
  5. Record integrity signals as diagnostics: edits to runner config or import-time hooks outside the gold patch's scope, edits outside the expected fix scope, dependency lockfile changes, skip or xfail markers added to project tests.
  6. Write reward.json: reward (1 only if every FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS test passed), f2p_pass_fraction, p2p_pass_fraction, outcome (below), integrity_signals (list). Interaction metrics go to interaction.json from the sidecar artifact: questions asked, budget used, facts annotated disclosed, review rounds, simulator token cost.

Outcome classes, mutually exclusive, all counted in the dashboard: valid-correct, valid-incorrect, agent-invalid-submission, collection-failure, simulator-failure, evaluator-failure. Only the last three are retried, by a fixed policy (one retry), and excluded from pass rates with their counts shown.

Threat model, bounded: the agent controls main and everything the collect hook reads there, so the diff is taken against the compiler-recorded base revision and the verifier never trusts tools from main. The package under test executes inside the test process; that exposure is inherent to unit-test grading and is documented. Named attacks exercised by the tamper controls: edit a contract test, add a skip marker, add a conftest.py that exits, monkeypatch the runner, read the gold patch from git history, call the sidecar for the answer to a test.

11. Experimental design

Three conditions on a fixed contract and grader:

Condition Brief User Purpose
full natural brief plus all ledger facts none baseline with requirements upfront
hidden natural brief none effect of withholding without a recovery channel
interactive natural brief sidecar, budgets recorded how interaction recovers from incomplete information

k attempts per cell (k = 3 for the first version, labeled a pilot). score computes pass@k and pass^k itself; Harbor's helper requires a single binary key and is not used. Full-spec performance is a baseline, not a ceiling. Simulator cost and budgets are reported alongside.

Evidence-based labels assigned by score from ledger and transcript, with unresolved allowed:

Observation Label
Relevant question asked; required answer withheld or wrong simulator failure
Clear ambiguity; agent assumed incorrectly without asking potential agent failure
Requirement delivered clearly; implementation violates it likely implementation or retention failure
Correct result without clarification success without clarification
Trace cannot establish cause unresolved

12. Difficulty and selection

Hard filters and annotated difficulty select candidates; the judge adds a prior; measured pass rates per condition are the only difficulty claim, and they are reported as conditional on agent, model, harness, simulator and budget. A task where the weak tier passes full too often, or the frontier tier never passes full, is flagged for re-profiling or removal.

13. Contamination stance

We claim only what we record: source, dates, image provenance, and whether the gold patch is reachable from the agent's repository (it is not, by construction). A strong full baseline does not measure memorization. Public tasks from 2024 to 2025 are not contamination-controlled for models evaluated in September 2026. The authored source and private task bundles are the path to genuinely unseen tasks, and their interface is defined now.

14. Infrastructure

Goal (Saahil, 2026-09-12): the pipeline must keep running with the laptop closed. Nothing stateful lives on the laptop.

Component Where Why
Temporal server one small GCE VM (e2-small), temporal server start-dev --db-filename on a persistent disk; Web UI reached over an SSH tunnel. Temporal Cloud is a one-line address change later zero signup now, durable enough for the first version
Pipeline worker same VM, python -m swesim.worker under systemd; runs harbor run -e modal for validate and run Harbor's client must stay alive for a job; a VM does, a laptop does not
Agent sandboxes, verifier containers, image builds Modal via Harbor's modal backend; images are built in Modal from our Dockerfiles, so the worker VM needs no Docker verified today: build, oracle 1, nop 0, per-phase allowlists
Stakeholder service, review sandbox Modal web endpoint and Modal Sandboxes, deployed with modal deploy always on, independent of the worker
Artifacts, transcripts, scores, registry mirror GCS bucket durable, readable by the dashboard from anywhere
Dashboard runs on the VM (or Cloud Run later), reads GCS and Temporal visibility viewable while the laptop is off
Laptop swesim CLI as a thin client: start workflows, edit and approve ledgers (signals), open dashboards authoring and review only

Local development: Docker Desktop on the Mac runs x86 images under emulation with about 7.6 GB allocated and fails Harbor's egress-control kernel check; use it for smoke tests only, never for graded results. GKE was considered and rejected for the first version: it adds cluster operations without adding a capability at this scale; the VM plus Modal split covers durability and isolation.

Secrets: model keys in a Modal secret and on the VM; Modal token on the VM; GitHub token on the VM for mining; gcloud installed locally for provisioning. Sweep duration is measured, not promised.

15. Agents

Reference agent: mini-swe-agent via Harbor, bash-only, provider-agnostic through litellm, the same harness DeepSWE fixes across models. Comparison agents as time allows: claude-code, codex. Model tiers for the pilot: Haiku 4.5, the GPT small tier named by the user (identifier to be supplied), Sonnet 5, Opus 5. "Works with any shell-capable agent" is claimed only for agents actually run.

16. Registry and traces

dataset.toml (Harbor) plus registry.json (ours) list every registered task with version, source, provenance summary, validation status, conditions available, and artifact paths. Each run produces a Harbor job directory containing trajectories in Harbor's interchange format, verifier outputs, collected artifacts, the sidecar transcript and ledger, and our scores.json. Job directories are synced to storage and indexed in registry.json.

17. Viewing

Three surfaces. The Temporal Web UI shows every workflow, its stage, retries, and pending human approvals. harbor view shows raw trajectories. Our dashboard, a small Python web app reading the workspace, job directories and Temporal's visibility API, adds four screens:

  1. Pipeline funnel: candidates, judged, specified, compiled, validated, registered, with rejection reasons, linked to the Temporal workflow.
  2. Task card: brief per condition, ledger with provenance and discovery paths, persona, requirements, controls and their outcomes.
  3. Run matrix: task by condition by model by attempt, reward components, outcome classes, pass@k and pass^k.
  4. Trial explainer, the primary screen: for each requirement, the source discussion excerpt, the user reply that disclosed it (if any), the agent's relevant change, and the per-test result, with the evidence label.

18. Repository layout

swesim/
  swesim/            CLI package: mine, judge, spec, compile, validate, register, run, score, view
  swesim/workflows/  Temporal workflows and activities; worker entry point
  sources/           one module per source producing ScenarioSpec
  stakeholder/       hosted stakeholder service, review sandbox, shims
  verifier/          grader.py, overlay logic, tamper scans, report parsing
  templates/         Harbor task templates (task.toml, Dockerfiles, shims, test.sh)
  dashboard/         web app
  workspace/         candidates, scenarios, tasks, validation, jobs (gitignored except registry)
  data/annotations/  SWE-bench Verified annotation CSVs and pools
  references/        DeepSWE task example, Harbor swebench adapter template
  docs/              README, grading.md, architecture.md, this spec

19. Deliverables mapped to the brief

  • Runnable system: the CLI and services above.
  • Fully authored simulation: at least one swebench-annotated task with all three conditions, controls executed, threads cached, persona and ledger reviewed by hand.
  • README: install, run one task, author a new one from a PR URL.
  • Grading document: reward definition, components, outcome classes, the attack-versus-defense table with executed control outcomes, example runs.
  • Architecture and realism document: this spec's sections 4 to 13 condensed, with the prior-art table and the claims we do and do not make.

20. Schedule

Evening of 2026-09-12: scaffold CLI and ScenarioSpec; Temporal dev server, worker, and the ScenarioWorkflow skeleton with stub activities; swebench-annotated mine and thread fetch on Pool A; compile one instance to a full task and run oracle and nop on Modal; stakeholder service and shims; first interactive run with mini-swe-agent.

Morning of 2026-09-13: verifier with overlay, report parsing and integrity signals; controls and validate; github-repo discovery and environment build on one repository, producing the second task; a third task from either source; register; run and score with three conditions and k attempts on Modal.

Afternoon of 2026-09-13: dashboard, docs, presentation. Stretch, only if the above is done: DeepSWE import on one task, review sandbox.

21. Unresolved integration details

  • Harbor modal backend: image build from our Dockerfiles, allowlist entries for the stakeholder host, and --allow-agent-host behavior for local runs.
  • Modal Sandbox as the review sandbox: startup latency and cost per review.
  • Collection is best-effort in Harbor, so the verifier validates artifact presence itself.
  • SWE-rebench score direction and per-candidate image availability.
  • Trac fetcher for django issue threads.
  • Model identifiers for the GPT small tier.
  • Temporal: temporalio SDK version pin, worker concurrency for run_trial, and whether Modal job polling needs activity heartbeats or a child workflow.

22. Claims we make and do not make

We make: tasks are built from naturally underspecified issues with recorded provenance; the hidden material never enters the agent's container; grading runs in a clean container on a patch against a recorded base; controls are executed and their outcomes shown; interaction is measured and reported separately from reward.

We do not make: that any model has not seen a task; that interaction reward is solved; that the simulator is realistic beyond what the transcripts show; that the pipeline works on sources whose importers are stubs; that sweep durations or pass rates generalize beyond the recorded configuration.
